Drake addressed a question about getting married when he was just 22 years old during Super Bowl media availability, explaining, “My teammates have the right to whatever they choose but I would definitely advise them to eventually get married. It’s one of the best things I’ve experienced in my life. There’s no better feeling than coming home to a wife that loves you and cares for you.”

He continued, “I know my teammates, some of them are experiencing different parts of their life. I chose to get married young, and I don’t regret it one bit.”

That same month, Ann Michael showed Drake some love after the Patriots lost Super Bowl 2026.

“Not how we wanted it to end but still thanking God for this incredible season❤️,” she wrote via Instagram on February 11, sharing photos from the big game. “We are blessed to be surrounded by such an amazing group of people, who made this season what it was. This is only the beginning!!”

After a whirlwind 2025-2026 football season, the Mayes jetted off to Japan for a well-earned vacation. Ann Michael documented their trip via social media in early March.

Drake and Ann Michael headed to Georgia to watch the 2026 Masters Tournament. “I love @themasters ⛳️💚,” she wrote via Instagram alongside several photos on the green with her husband.

Shortly after their 1st wedding anniversary, Ann Michael opened up about the most significant obstacle the couple has been forced to navigate during married life.

“Moving to somewhere so completely different, being away from all of our friends and family is probably the most challenging part,” she exclusively told Us. “Luckily, we have great teammates and great friends here that have really made the New England area feel like home, which is great.”

She continued, “But you know, we’re both from North Carolina. Our parents live in the same neighborhood, and then we went to college in North Carolina, so we were never too far from family. That’s been the biggest adjustment.”

After Drake suffered an ankle injury during the Patriots game against the Detroit Lions in Munich, Germany, on November 15, Ann Michael showed her husband support via social media.

“ILY always,” she wrote via her Instagram Story on November 17, alongside a red heart emoji. Ann Michael also shared a photo of the couple kissing before Drake took the field in Europe.

Drake exited the game after being sacked in the first quarter. The team hadn’t revealed his official diagnosis or timeline for recovery at the time of Ann Michael’s post.

#3569. This GTA 6-Inspired Keycap Set Will Make The Wait For A PC Version Slightly Easier

Grand Theft Auto 6 is now just a couple of hours away in some parts of the world. That is, if you're planning to play on either Xbox or PlayStation. The wait for a PC version is still ongoing, with Rockstar yet to indicate when it plans to release that port. In the meantime, however, you can start ensuring that your setup is at least ready for when it arrives.

High-end keycap manufacturer GMK has revealed a new set that is clearly inspired by GTA 6 and Vice City, without explicitly mentioning either. The new set, named Neon Vice, features black keycaps with an array of colored alphas and numerical keys, all drawing from the pink, orange, and purple colors of Rockstar's impending sequel. Novelty keycaps include images of speedboats across choppy water, palm trees, and alligators, and the Vice City skyline.

Like most GMK sets, the keycaps are constructed from double-shot ABS plastic, which should ensure fantastic legibility with use over time. What isn't normal is the price, however. GMK keycap sets are priced at a premium, and Neon Vice is no exception. Expect to pay $170 for the base kit, and an additional $45 if you want the novelty keys on top of that. Preorders open for the kit today across multiple vendors around the world.

That's a lot more than the game itself, so if you haven't been bitten by the custom keyboard bug, it's probably best to just continue waiting. Thankfully the gap between console and PC versions for GTA 6 might not be as large as previous Rockstar titles, with a report suggesting that it might arrive in early 2027. If you are playing on console you can pre-load the game right now ahead of its launch, which will start for lucky players in New Zealand very soon.

Anticipation has been building for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth for months, and the first reactions are in. Fans of Quentin Tarantino, Brad Pitt, and David Fincher, like me, can rest easy. I’ve been excited for this since I first learned the three would team up for the movie, which will be available with a Netflix subscription on December 23, but will run for two weeks in theaters starting November 25 as part of the 2026 movie schedule. Now that the first reactions are hitting social media after the movie premiered last night in Los Angeles,

I’m even more excited, especially after reading one review that subtly referred to the Tarantino-Fincher pairing as my favorite candy, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups. Drew Taylor, who writes for The Wrap, summed it up perfectly, saying the writer and director are “like peanut butter and chocolate”:

Absolutely loved #CliffBooth — Tarantino and Fincher are like peanut butter and chocolate (the peanut butter is profane and the chocolate dipped in blood). Stop watching anything, go see it on the biggest screen around, have the time of your life. An absolute triumph. The best. https://t.co/6uUNnHPjyINovember 17, 2026

Taylor is not alone in his praise, either. Many are lauding the combination of the two, who came together on this sort-of-kinda-sequel to Tarantino’s 2019 smash hit Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood, which earned Brad Pitt his first Academy Award and is, in my opinion, Tarantino’s best movie since Pulp Fiction (hot take, I know). Courtney Howard, a writer for Variety and other outlets, calls the movie a great “hang out” film, giving flowers to Pitt and his co-stars Elizabeth Debicki and Peter Weller:

THE FURTHER MISADVENTURES OF #CLIFFBOOTH is a pure riot. David Fincher’s play at a nostalgic bygone era Quentin Tarantino loves works like gangbusters. Takes time to form, but plays like a LA film noir hangout picture. Pitt & Debicki are electric together. Peter Weller, MVP. https://t.co/njhxWdSm0fNovember 17, 2026

“Hangout” movies are among my favorite styles of movies. When they are done well, like Dazed and Confused or most of my favorite Tarantino movies (Once Upon a Time, Jackie Brown, etc.), they often become the movies I return to over and over. This seems to be another one of those. Clayton Davis, another Variety writer, also calls it one:

David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a wild, hilarious hangout movie. Brad Pitt slides back into his beloved Oscar-winning role and gives his best performance since “Once Upon a Time in...Hollywood.” Elizabeth Debicki brings an intoxicating sensuality, and Scott Caan and Peter Weller are such a treat that they could have had triple the screen time. The cinematography is gorgeous. If the 2019 film was a love letter to L.A., this one is a full-on sonnet. It’s also a nice reminder that not every director needs to write their own films, and not every writer needs to direct them. Fincher and Tarantino haven’t been this much fun in years. #CliffBooth #netflixfilm #OscarsNovember 17, 2026

Critic Josh Blumenkranz also leans into the hangout aspect of the movie, and again praises the supporting cast, including Debicki and Scott Caan:

THE FURTHER MISADVENTURES OF CLIFF BOOTH a hilarious, violent, and cool hangout movie. Brad Pitt is charming as ever as Cliff Booth. Welcome additions Elizabeth Debicki and Scott Caan also deliver. Not as good as Once but still a fun time. Love letter to Los Angeles! #cliffbooth https://t.co/lMosyYBFI0November 17, 2026

Debicki, who is probably best known for playing Princess Diana in The Crown, is getting a ton of love, with some saying she “stuns” and Jazz Tangcay from Variety calling her the MVP of the movie:

Elizabeth Debicki in #CliffBooth she doesn’t miss and is one of the film’s MVP https://t.co/yulGVidzWcNovember 17, 2026

Pretty much every reaction that I’ve read this morning is glowing, even when critics don’t think it’s as good as Once Upon a Time. Simon Thompson posted:

David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of #CliffBooth pops, throbs and crackles. Like Once Upon a Time… this is a love letter to LA. An eclectic, ragtag cast make this a slick and sexy romp. A salty and slower-burning side piece to Tarantino’s original with a fire final act. https://t.co/3izap5l2wpNovember 17, 2026

He also called it a “love letter” to Hollywood, which was the descriptor that many would hang on the first movie starring Pitt as the stuntman Cliff Booth alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. DiCaprio doesn’t appear in this one, nor do the other stars of the Tarantino classic, like Margot Robbie. This is Brad Pitt and Elizabeth Debicki, according to the reviews, and that is A-OK with me.

Could this movie land another Oscar nomination for Pitt? It’s not often that an actor gets a nomination twice for the same role, as Al Pacino did for playing Michael Corleone in the first two Godfather films. It sounds like that is definitely on the table here. I really can’t wait to check out what sounds like a really fun movie in IMAX next month.

#3567. These Are Some Of The Biggest Snubs At The Game Awards 2026

The nominees for The Game Awards have been announced. Some of the biggest games--and those that aren't out yet--make appearances on the list, including Grand Theft Auto 6 and Phantom Blade Zero, but some of the games could've--and maybe should've--been nominated in multiple categories. So, let's go over some of the biggest snubs at this year's TGAs.

Let's start with the big one: Game of the Year. You've got six games nominated here: 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Grand Theft Auto 6, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. All of them are fabulous and well-deserved, but a couple of games are missing: House House's co-op adventure Big Walk and Rebel Wolves' vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker. They appear elsewhere, sure, but I think they deserve GOTY contention, as well.

Let's move onto Best Performance. You've got some stellar voice work here: Angela Sant’Albano as Grace Ashcroft in Resident Evil Requiem, Liam McIntyre as James "Logan" Howlett in Marvel's Wolverine, Manni L. Perez as Lucia Caminos in GTA 6, Patrick Gibson as James Bond in 007 First Light, and Rahul Kohli as Arjun Devraj in Saros. Not taking anything away from these incredible voice talents, but Nick Apostolides as Leon Kennedy in Resident Evil Requiem, Sean Durrie as Dylan Faden in Control Resonant, and Will de Renzy-Martin as Coen in The Blood of Dawnwalker deserve some recognition, too.

Marathon could've easily been nominated for Best Art Direction and Best Action Game. Overwatch and WoW/WoW: Forever would've made sense in the Best Ongoing Game category. Denshattack's soundtrack is too good not to be nominated for Best Score and Music. And Castlevania: Belmont's Curse could slot into a number of categories, including Best Action/Adventure Game, Best Art Direction, and Best Narrative.

There are probably many others that have come out this year that maybe could--and maybe should--have been nominated but weren't for one reason or another. (Note: GameSpot is among the publications that contribute to the nomination process.)

Regardless, we won't have to wait too long to learn what games win what categories, as The Game Awards will air live on December 10 at 4:30 PM PT / 7:30 PM ET.

#3566. Stacey Abrams in Conversation With Ta-Nehisi Coates

When I first met Stacey Abrams in 2015, she passed on to me the message that she was then passing on to anyone who’d listen: Someday soon, Georgia would be blue. This struck me as unlikely. But three years later Abrams ran for governor, and shocked the country by coming within two points of winning. Then two years later, when Joe Biden sealed his presidential election in 2020 with a win in Georgia, and Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff won Senate seats, Abrams looked prophetic. Now, Democrats have gone beyond Georgia, penetrating into the deepest reaches of the South—Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. To understand how the GOP’s Solid South grew brittle, I could think of no better person to talk to than Abrams.

The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Ta-Nehisi Coates: My recollection of our first meeting goes back to 2015, when I was promoting Between the World and Me. You interviewed me for the book. We had a wonderful discussion. My family was actually in the audience, because, like all Black folks, I have family in Atlanta. They were so excited. I was talking to Stacey Abrams—Minority Leader Stacey Abrams. And one of the things you said backstage was, “We’re going to make Georgia blue.” And I don’t know that I scoffed at you. I like to think I wasn’t quite that rude.

Stacey Abrams: Your eyebrow arched a bit.

I confess to the eyebrow arching. And so the eyebrow arched and you made the case. Can you tell me what you saw?

I’d gone through redistricting, and one of the component pieces of redistricting, of course, is that it’s predicated on the census. The US census is a tool that is incredibly powerful and deeply inexact. It was the first time Republicans had power to draw the lines since Reconstruction. And I took a posture in my caucus, and it was this: “If you vote for their maps, I will come after your seats.” And I was not only unequivocal in saying it, I wrote it down because I didn’t want anyone to misquote me.

In order to take that posture, I had to read the maps myself. And what I saw was that Republicans were placing bets that, by drawing the lines a certain way, they were going to give themselves 124 of 180 seats. So 67% of the seats, even though they’d only won the election by 57%.

But I looked at those same maps and I’m like, In this place, in this part of Paulding County, there is a new subdivision that is predominantly Black. And in this part of Gwinnett County, there is a burgeoning Korean population that is now going into its second generation, which means a lot of those will be eligible voters. And down in South Georgia, you have third-generation migrant farm workers who are Latino, but who have decided to plant their roots here and raise their families here. When you looked at those numbers, the maps had a very different story to tell about Republican dominance: They could win for a decade. They could not win for a generation.

We tell ourselves stories about the information we get, and people repeat stories without ever reading it themselves. There are a lot of people who can quote Tom Sawyer who’ve never read the book. And so in our politics, that happens a lot, that the story that becomes popular doesn’t ever get traced back to its origin or to the original text.

What I saw in Georgia is true in Louisiana, in Mississippi, in Tennessee, in Alabama, in South Carolina. We just saw it happen in North Carolina.

So when you saw this wave of redistricting happening around the country this year, did you see a similar opportunity?

Oh, absolutely. I was in Tennessee the day that they passed the maps and what stuck out for me was Raumesh Akbari, who’s the Senate minority leader, she asked to see the bill, and the Republican chair of the committee said, “Well, we don’t have a bill yet, but we know what it’s going to say.” They planned to vote on it even though they did not have the text of the bill.

The Republicans were moving so fast because they thought they understood what they were pulling together. Justin Pearson didn’t pick up the seat he wanted, but they were at risk of losing a seat they thought was going to be theirs because they misread the topography, but they didn’t do a deeper dive into exactly what was laying in the crevices. And that’s where opportunity for us is born.

There are not enough Black people to win any single seat outright on their own in most legislative districts, and no statewide elections, especially post–Louisiana v. Callais, but there are coalitions that can be built. And what I saw from the very beginning was the possibility of coalition.

What I see for the South, what I think the South proved on Tuesday, is the possibility of coalition, but coalition does not happen without conflict. It does not happen without conversation, and it does not happen when we have convinced ourselves of the permanence of our second-class citizenship and our subjugation. What we saw on Tuesday was a moment where people realized that the power to improve their own lives had become so desperately thin that they had to use it or lose it. We cannot rely on that for the next two years.

What I hear you saying is that the last two years created an emergency. But that can’t be depended on. It can’t be “The Most Important Election of Our Lifetime” every two years. Desperation is not enough.

It can’t be. Desperation gets you one moment. There’s a whole body of medical research on people that have heart attacks and they get saved. And what it shows is that they are exercise fiends for about six weeks and then they fall back into their patterns because it’s a normalcy bias.

If we constantly feel on the edge of danger, we cannot function. And so we reorient our understanding of normal to survive. And therefore our responsibility in this moment is to look at the opportunity that was revealed on Tuesday, but not read into it that that opportunity either requires desperation or it requires this milquetoast approach, because our default is not just normalcy, but the most banal form of normalcy we can imagine.

I know you have some concerns about some of the narratives emerging out of the midterms. Would you talk a bit about that?

I saw something on Axios that I think was well-intentioned and it essentially said that the threats to our democracy were overblown, that our courts held, that our Congress held, that our presidency wasn’t overreaching, and that for normal people, things were fine. How have we reached the place where we think it is normal that the capital city in the United States of America is under military occupation? How is it okay that the courts held when it permits the incarceration of children in Dilley, Texas, and the kidnapping of people of color because of race and the language that they speak? There is something aggressively privileged about this idea that democracy is not in jeopardy because those who are the most protected don’t feel harm.

But Tuesday was a repudiation of this idea that things are normal. You saw turnout at extraordinary levels from a cross section of communities, almost all of whom have been directly impacted by the harms of this administration. Not just the economic harms that hit everyone, but harms that were amplified and refined for their cruelty.

At the same time, there’s a worry that I have that, because we won control of Congress for the patriots—and that’s how I frame it, I no longer think it’s just Democrat versus Republican, it’s patriots versus authoritarians—even though the patriots may have gained more purchase in Congress, we still have a Supreme Court that gutted the last vestiges of protection for the Voting Rights Act. We still have a Supreme Court that stripped women of their bodily autonomy. We still have a Supreme Court that has said that protections that are afforded by DEI are somehow suspect. And when those are true, then the successes of Tuesday don’t signal that we’ve won. They signal that we have to work even harder because the harms have not dissipated, they just haven’t penetrated.

You said something a few months back that’s stuck with me—that our elections are ripe for entertainment. As a sports fan, I think it’s not a coincidence that so many sports figures are now commenting on politics because the way they appear on TV is actually quite similar to the way sports appears. You have these long campaigns, which is like your season. Then you have primaries, which are like your playoffs, and then you have this big Super Bowl that happens on Tuesday. And so, it’s an entertainment and ratings bonanza. And I think, as I recall, you were cautioning against that as a view of politics. Can you speak a little bit more about that?

Yeah. When you think about politics, if you think about elections as an event, and to extend your analogy, if the elections are the finals, if the elections are game seven, if it’s the Super Bowl, when that happens, then the day after, you go home, the game is over. But the challenge I have is that it’s not just that we treat it as a sporting event, it’s that we treat politics as though we are spectators at a sporting event. And when we look at the other party, it’s like we are spectators watching a very disciplined, seasoned team that practices in the off-season, that travels together, that plays overseas. They’re constantly engaged and we are on and off. We think of politics, again, as entertainment as opposed to the job.

How did we end up with this entertainment narrative?

Theodore White did this series where he examined elections 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972. And when you read it, as someone who is reading it in the 21st century, the arc of how we have viewed politics changed dramatically, specifically in 1960 with the advent of television, because the election contest between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon hinged in no small part on that televised debate. And I think for you and me and for anyone who wasn’t old enough to see it, I did not realize that it was one of the most watched programs in American history. We take for granted how many people are going to watch the debates these days, but with that first debate, it was one of the most watched programs in the world because it had never happened before. And the moment it became a television spectacle, it became entertainment because you were watching, you picked winners and losers, you picked your villain and you picked your champion.

It’s human nature, we put things into these narrative arcs. As someone who writes comic books, you understand this. As someone who writes thrillers, I think about this. You create a villain, you have a protagonist, an antagonist, you have to have a storyline, you have to have complications, and when television became the medium, it added a layer and a texture to what had long been the mechanics of politics. Then you add into it the drama of Black and brown people getting to participate. And then you layer on top of that “blue state versus red state,” and the sharp division, and the attribution to entire regions of a value system and a personality based on a single day.

What would it mean to remain engaged beyond elections? When I think about the conservative movement, I think about the degree to which the religious right is engaged. I think about Trump rallies. I think people were baffled by this at first—the clothes, the trucks, the boats. But what I would say is those are markers of community. They aren’t my politics. But they seem part of something larger than a particular bill or policy.

There’s a lot of talk in organizing about going for belief first, or belonging first. On the left, we are often accused of belief, that you have to be in line with all of our ideas, our values, our ideologies, but also the tactical, practical ways of exercising them, and that because we say you have to believe first, we filter out people who haven’t had time to understand or adapt or even decide what they believe. The right uses belonging. They say, “Come and be a part of us, and we’ll tell you what we are.” So you get the jersey, you get the cap, you get the red, you get to use the language, even if you haven’t decided that you actually believe all they believe, which is why you have people who are suddenly surprised that this is what happened.

We have to shift. Not to say that we don’t have beliefs, but we have to give people time to grow into those beliefs. I come at this from my time as minority leader. I had a caucus of 60 members in a chamber of 180, and my members included suburban white mothers and rural Black pastors and everything in between. We were the most racially diverse caucus. We were geographically diverse. And I had no power. I was the minority leader. My job was to help harmonize their approach. I could not lead with belief, because people were entitled to their beliefs, but my job was to bring them into belonging first because they were members of the caucus. And then my second job was to make sure that anyone who needed them to believe something had the platform to offer the tutelage.

That’s the place where I think we are failing. We don’t do the tutelage. We say, “There has been a conversation, this is now our truth. And if you don’t adopt that truth, you are somehow opposed to it,” as opposed to, “You haven’t adopted the truth because you don’t know what it means and you don’t understand it and you haven’t experienced it. Let me give you time and space to come in,” or, “You have legitimate disagreement, and maybe on this, we will not be in alignment, but your disagreement should not lead to hostility against my community.”

The Democratic Socialists of America have attracted a lot of attention recently, but one thing they seem to do is this “belonging” piece. I can’t say I understood this before, but I was talking to someone for a story, and then mentioned the social environment. So here in New York, when people go out to canvas, afterwards, they all go out for beers. The beers are not really the point, but making people feel like they belong to something is.

Yeah. I mean, what they are doing is what works in most effective social movements. During the Vietnam War, one of the most effective protest waves happened at coffee shops. You brought people together around the table, they got to vent about what they were upset about, they went out and protested and then they came back together. People like being liked.

In terms of belief, how does one do that and not make those who are in that coalition who are particularly vulnerable feel abandoned? Obviously, I mean, this is not the only case, but I’m thinking about the tremendous amount of negative attention brought on the trans community. What do you do when the “belonging” comes in conflict with actually protecting the members of your coalition?

My first position is, if you have a faith that tells you it is okay to cause harm because you feel uncomfortable, I need to understand where your faith lies. Our first responsibility is the protection of difference. And it is to say you don’t have to embrace, but you cannot lift up pitchforks. You cannot demonize, you cannot revile, you cannot scapegoat because all of those are hostile actions of cruelty that not only cause harm to the victim, they diminish your ability to learn. So the worry I have is that too often we sacrifice that education piece because it’s uncomfortable and because it requires defending those you may not be in complete alignment with, and it’s an easier thing to just jump on the bandwagon.

In my caucus, when I was a minority leader, another issue I had was abortion, and I had two members who were pastors. I was not going to be able to change their ideological position and I wasn’t going to try. But I had these members walk off the floor, instead of voting, on abortion bills. And there were some who got mad and they’re like, “Oh, we should know their position.” I said, “A yes vote on this bill causes harm, and no vote is a help. Not voting is the same as a no vote. So why do you need them to make a declaration when their declaration of refusing to do harm is progress?” So there’s a complexity that we often elide because we failed to measure what harm looks like, and the path from good to harm is a lot shorter than we want to believe.

Did you work with Angie Nixon during her race?

I feel like she excited a certain element of the base in a way that we haven’t really seen before.

I contributed and then I went down to Florida, actually did an event at Florida A&M University and did one at Cafe Resistance. I got to know her mama. I knew of her as a state representative. And when I decided to support her campaign, it was because she has always put the work of serving people first. She has built networks, but more importantly, she solves problems.

When Florida started banning books, she started a bookstore for banned books. That kind of tactical response with strategic intention is often lacking and it has been part of how I try to operate. We’ve got people who are good at being diagnosticians and we’ve got folks who can offer prescriptions and we’ve got people who can actually administer the medicine. And we need more people who are willing to do all three. You need people who are specialists; I’m not saying you don’t, but what she has demonstrated is the capacity to do the three.

Have you heard some of the negative commentary after the election about her campaign? I’m thinking about James Carville, for instance—this notion that somehow she was a poor fit for Florida or was a bad candidate. It’s not great. Have you seen any of this?

Well, I have thoughts on the fact that we keep thinking the solution to the problem is the thing that failed before. And I believe in experimentation. If you look at my history, I have never been top of mind as the solution to problems. And some of it is timing, some of it is capacity, and some of it is helping change the public imagination, but we’re never going to get what we need if we only use what we’ve always had.

I just find it interesting that she is attracting negative commentary, from certain quarters, in a way that David Jolly is not, even though they both lost and the margin wasn’t that much between the two of them. She came very, very close to winning, in a state Democrats really didn’t expect to compete in two years ago. And look, I just have to say, you are somebody who in 2018 came really, really close too. You’re both Black women. I just wonder what you make of the critique.

The critique is easy because Angie Nixon is different. She’s different than what they are used to, and she is different than 250 years of expectation has led us to presume is right. I am excited about Juliana Stratton and Angela Alsobrooks and Lisa Blunt Rochester being in the US Senate. That is an extraordinary thing. Adding Angie Nixon would’ve been an amazing, amazing addition. But for pundits whose sense of success is grounded in past history, she strains the imagination.

David Jolly ran a smart race. Angie Nixon ran a smart race, and we know that because they came close to winning, but you are never entitled to victory. You are entitled to effort. And this notion that there is some magical formula for what wins in the South got completely obliterated yesterday when Scott Colom won a seat that we haven’t held since 1874. We know that what can win is a combination of a smart candidate, an invested campaign, and an electorate who sees and hears themselves in the story told.

Angie didn’t get that opportunity because she had a late primary and no resources. And to judge her using a metric that was never designed for her is deeply problematic. And it’s not just about her being a Black woman, it’s about how do we win an evolving electorate if all we know is to do what we’ve always done? And so my argument for the Democratic Party is that our notions of electability have to evolve with the democracy that we deserve and that we design, and it cannot be anchored to these sometimes antiquated notions that the only thing we can do is not lose as opposed to let’s try really hard to win by meeting the moment. And I think Angie Nixon did an incredible job of meeting the moment.

And what about you—do you still have ambitions for public office?

Do you worry that some of the work you do as a kind of public political strategist (like in this interview, frankly) will conflict at all? When I think about people seeking office, they often try to say as little as possible.

Politics is a tool. It is not an identity for me. It’s a tool. And that’s different. And there are people for whom this is what they do and we need those people. This is not a disparaging comment about others, but for me, it is a tool. It is one of the ways to do the work I believe needs to be done. I think that poverty is immoral. I think it is solvable. I think it is economically inefficient. And for most of my life, the work for me has been about how do you solve this economic poverty? When I got deep in the work, I realized that we also had a moral poverty that we had to contend with, and we have this poverty of imagination. And the problem is you cannot convince people to believe that their problems can be solved if you won’t talk about them.

And in the South, silence is protective. It has been a way to nibble around the edges, but the only people who could be loud about it were the people who could afford volume. And politicians rarely can afford volume. I want things to be better and I’m not willing to forgo any tool that will make that happen. But I’m also not willing to protect my future opportunities by rejecting my current responsibilities.

#3565. 007 First Light Might Be The End Of The Line For James Bond’s Favorite Watch

After months of searching and numerous potential frontrunners, Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond. It's lead to some questions about whether he's too famous or too old for the role, whether or not he looks like Bond, and just how different his portrayal might be to those that came before him. For some others, however, the questions is far more direct: What watch is he going to wear?

James Bond has long had recognizable brand associations, but one that has endured has been the partnership with luxury watch maker Omega. Bond was first seen wearing an Omega in 1995's GoldenEye, and was mostly recently seen sporting the latest iteration of the Seamaster Diver 300m in this year's 007 First Light. Although not a new film in the series, First Light still featured its own unique take on the Seamaster, the first ever created for a videogame, with Omega adding it to its bursting 007 collection that it makes available for purchase.

So given that it's been three decades, why could First Light be the last iteration of James Bond wearing an Omega? Simply put, Robert Pattinson doesn't wear one, and has very recently become a brand ambassador for one of Omega's Swiss competitors, Jaeger-LeCoultre. There's no confirmation that Pattinson's obligations will directly influence a brand deal between Omega and new Bond owners Amazon, but the omission of any watch at all in the announcement trailer sure has cause some speculation.

Daniel Craig, during his tenure as Bond, was Omega's chief ambassador, often wearing unreleased models to drum up interest for imminent releases. That might not be the case with Pattinson, which could suggest a change for what timepiece his Bond decides to switch to.

If Bond were to jump from Omega to JLC, it would be somewhat fitting. The watch maker manufactures some extremely elegant pieces with a rich history associated with each line. But none makes as much sense as the rectangular Reverso. The watch is distinct in its design, allowing the wearer to rotate the face and flip it 180 degrees, with a variety of designs on the back. Initially created for polo players to protect their prized wristwatches, you can clearly see a lot of potential for some weird and creative Bond gadgetry to intersect with a design like this.

Or maybe Pattinson will arrive on the block with yet another Seamaster Diver 300m, and all of this would've been wishful thinking. But if he doesn't, and this truly is the last we'll see of Bond with Omega, at least First Light introduced one of the better entries in the entire collection.

#3564. Patrick Mahomes and Wife Brittany Announce Sex of Baby No. 4 With Cake Reveal

Patrick Mahomes and wife Brittany Mahomes have revealed the gender of their fourth child.

“Baby #4🥹🤭,” the Chiefs quarterback, 31, and Brittany, also 31, teased via a joint Instagram video shared on Tuesday, November 17. In the video, the couple were seen in a kitchen with a white cake topped with tiny pink and blue frosted flowers and the words “Oh baby.”

Holding a champagne glass each, the couple, joined by their three children — daughters Sterling, 5, and Golden, 22 months, and son Bronze, 3 — shared a sweet kiss before dunking the tops of their glasses into the cake to see which color frosting would appear once the glassware was retrieved.

To their delight, blue sugary goodness coated the rims of each glass, indicating that they will be welcoming a second son next year.

While Patrick grinned widely over the reveal, Brittany shared her own joy by pounding her fists in the air and jumping up and down. In the meantime, the couple’s family popped confetti cannons that sprayed blue and gold.

The duo then shared another kiss before giving their children hugs, with Brittany raising an arm in the air and Patrick lifting Bronze up high for the cameras.

The clip concluded with further footage of the children making snow angels out of the fallen confetti on the ground before Patrick’s mom, Randi Mahomes, was seen hugging Brittany’s mom, Diana Lindeberg, and the entire clan posed for photos together.

Brittany and Patrick announced on Tuesday, November 10, that they were expanding their brood once again. “Another blessing from God🥹🙏🏼,” they wrote in a joint Instagram post. “& then there were 6🤍.”

Two days later, Patrick said during a Chiefs press conference that he was hoping for a boy. “Obviously, it’s a blessing to have another baby on the way. I’m excited for it,” he said at the time. “I’m hoping that me and Bronze can even up the score.”

He added that besides the baby’s gender, he was mostly “praying for a healthy baby at the end of the day.”

After a reporter pointed out that every time the couple have made a pregnancy announcement in the past, the Chiefs have ended their season with a Super Bowl. The comment put another smile on Patrick’s face.

“I’m hoping. I don’t know if Brittany is,” Patrick responded with a laugh. “But I’m hoping if we can keep that going and get another Super Bowl win with a baby on the way that’d be awesome for sure.”

Robert Pattinson has had a pretty ridiculous year. Between The Drama, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, and the upcoming Dune: Part Three on the 2026 movie schedule, he's been keeping busy. Now, as if playing the Dark Knight wasn't enough, he's officially been cast as the next James Bond. Naturally, the announcement has generated plenty of reactions, but I wasn't expecting Jon Stewart to have one of the funniest takes I've heard so far.

During Monday night's episode of The Daily Show, Stewart addressed the Bond casting while discussing a string of technological disasters and travel disruptions that had made headlines over the weekend. Somehow, he wove them all into an increasingly ridiculous story about how he was supposed to audition for 007. The lengths he went to before revealing that the Twilight franchise breakout star had beaten him to the role had me laughing out loud. Stewart joked:

I was supposed to fly out to a gig. An audition, actually. Kind of a big one. And obviously, delays at the airport. No big deal. I just thought, well, I'll just go by my preferred travel method, Mississippi riverboat.

When your flight gets canceled, logic dictates that the next step is to hop aboard a riverboat. Obviously. Unfortunately for Stewart, his backup transportation wasn't particularly reliable either, and things only got worse when he tried to contact the people running the audition. He continued the bit:

Unfortunately, we also ran into a bit of a... well, it ran into us, but... so I just thought, well, I'll let the production know I was going to be late by sending them an email from my beloved Microsoft Outlook account. And then the... uh... which... it would have been fine, as long as I could still electronically withdraw the money to rent a car, which... long story short, they ended up giving the role to [BLEEP] Robert Pattinson.

I was already laughing at the idea of Stewart missing out on a big role because his riverboat ran into trouble and Microsoft Outlook wasn't cooperating. But he saved his best complaint for last, taking issue with the fact that Pattinson already has another pretty famous character on his résumé. Raising his fist in mock frustration, the longtime late-night host shouted:

Pattinson! You already got Batman. Enough's enough!

I mean, he's got a point. How many iconic characters does one guy need? Here's an actor who has already played Edward Cullen in the Twilight movies, Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter, and Bruce Wayne in The Batman. Now he's adding 007 to the résumé. At this rate, I half expect someone to announce him as the next Superman. Hey, with James Gunn’s recent outing anything is possible.

Of course, Stewart was having fun with the news, and I don't think anybody seriously believes Pattinson should be disqualified from playing Bond because he's already Batman. But I do think it's funny that the actor is becoming the face of another enormous franchise while he's still working on The Batman: Part II.

Pattinson's casting as James Bond was officially announced Monday, following years of speculation about who would replace Daniel Craig. The upcoming 26th Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who also worked with the Die My Darling actor on Dune: Part Three. While plenty of actors were rumored to be in contention, Pattinson ultimately landed the role. The announcement has already generated strong reactions from fans, which is hardly surprising given how attached people are to the franchise.

Personally, I'm curious to see what he brings to Bond. He's spent years choosing interesting projects and taking roles that don't always seem like the obvious next step for somebody who became famous playing a sparkly vampire. His Batman was a particularly interesting take on Bruce Wayne, and I wouldn't be surprised if he approached 007 with the same willingness to make the character his own. Although now I also kind of want to hear him deliver the famous Bond introduction in his Batman voice.

Robert Pattinson's first James Bond movie doesn't have a release date yet, although production is expected to begin sometime in 2027. Meanwhile, The Batman: Part II is currently scheduled for February 2028.

Personally, I think it would be hilarious if Pattinson's next role was playing Jon Stewart in a biopic. Stranger things have happened in Hollywood, and at this point, Stewart might want to keep an eye on those casting announcements.

In the meantime, you can catch Stewart hosting The Daily Show Mondays at 11 p.m. ET on Comedy Central, with new episodes available to stream the following morning with a Paramount+ subscription.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3562. Civilization Dev Lays Off 1/3 Of Staff, New XCOM Game Facing “Development Struggles” – Report

The video game industry's woes continue as Take-Two's 2K division has confirmed that one third of the staff at Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis Games is being laid off.

Bloomberg confirmed the cuts, which will impact around 60 people. As part of the downsizing, Firaxis studio head Heather Hazen is leaving.

A spokesperson for Firaxis confirmed the restructuring to Bloomberg, saying the cuts are part of an effort to "focus on design, technology, and player experience."

"These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis," the spokesperson said.

According to Bloomberg's sources, Firaxis is working on a new XCOM game, but it has faced "development struggles" and missed a major milestone this past summer. The game is still going ahead, though the sources said it "may face a shakeup" due to the layoffs.

The latest game from Firaxis, Sid Meier's Civilization VII, was released in February 2025 and had numerous technical issues upon release, though the experience has been improved since then with updates. The entire Civilization series has sold more than 80 million units.

As for the XCOM series, the latest entry from Firaxis was 2020's XCOM: Chimera Squad, and before that was 2016's XCOM 2.

Firaxis was co-founded by Sid Meier in 1996, so 2026 is the studio's 30th anniversary. Take-Two bought the company in 2005 and put the studio and the franchise under the 2K banner.

#3561. Everything You Missed at Vanity Fair's Screening Room Los Angeles

Not even a nationwide FAA ground stop could prevent movie stars from descending upon Los Angeles for the Governor Awards and Vanity Fair's first annual Screening Room this past weekend. Hosted at LACMA's brand-new Steve Tisch theater, actors including Matt Damon, Penélope Cruz, Pedro Pascal, Andrew Garfield, John Leguizamo, and Andrew Scott joined Q&As to discuss their films and pressing topics in the entertainment industry. AI was a major theme throughout the weekend, and not just at the screening for Artificial, as actors and directors spoke about the desire to continue making things that feel “real” and “made by humans.” Following each screening, talent mingled with guests to continue the conversations.

The weekend began with a screening of Wild Horse Nine, director Martin McDonagh's dark comedy starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents behind the plan to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973. Following the showing, VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford led a Q&A with McDonagh, Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, who also stars in the film.

Next up was Elsinore, which tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (played by Andrew Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. In conversation with VF's Rebecca Ford, Scott, his costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, Scott discussed what it was like to tell Charleson's story. “I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” he said.

Come Friday night, audiences gathered for a screening of the acclaimed Spanish language drama La Bola Negra, which follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War. It stars Miguel Bernardeau, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo (the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente) in his first major acting role, Carlos Gonzalez, Milo Quifes and Penélope Cruz.

After the film, Ricky Martin moderated a panel conversation featuring directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, and stars Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau. Calvo talked about how they are all riding high on the film's positive reception. “Creating this sense of community and hearing people saying, ‘This movie changed me. It really made me understand things about me.’ The power that art has, we forget it, but then this happens and … the rest is a dream. The rest we're living is a dream.”

Saturday's slate of programming began with a live recording of Vanity Fair's “Notes on a Scene” with Matt Damon, John Leguizamo and Himesh Patel, who recounted what it was like to film The Odyssey with director Christopher Nolan. Next, Seth Rogen joined Screening Room for “Scene Selection,” taking the audience through what it was like shooting Freaks and Geeks, Knocked Up, The Studio and more.

Later that afternoon, Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy joined the festivities following a screening of their new film Behemoth!, which tells the story of a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and to score films after decades performing symphonic work around the country. In conversation with VF's West Coast Editor John Ross for Behemoth!, Pascal spoke about how making the film gave him “a tremendous amount of hope.” “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious," he said.

Come Saturday night, guests were eager to see Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, which follows the rise of OpenAI and a few of its pioneers: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati. Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation with VF's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci. “It's important to try to understand because as Luca said, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. And we've kind of given our autonomy over or it's been taken from behind our backs,” Garfield said.

On Sunday, Cruz joined director Florian Zeller for a screening of the film Bunker, a timely film about a famous architect, played by Javier Bardem, and his wife Sofia, played by Cruz, who is asked to build a bunker for a tech giant. This sparks a rift in their marriage as the couple examines how success and monetary gain have affected their lives. Cruz, who is having a huge year with The Invite and La Bola Negra alongside this film, expressed her excitement that younger audiences are coming back to theaters and are looking for films that don't “over-explain."

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room paired this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that included post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

Harry Shum Jr. looked back on his experience filming Glee during the latest episode of Dancing With the Stars.

“I feel like Dancing With the Stars is synonymous with glee … and to be able to dance to Naya’s version, it means so much to so many people, including myself. We miss you, baby girl,” Shum, 44, said during the semifinals on Tuesday, November 17, after his second dance of the night.

After starting the show with a paso doble to “We Found Love” by Rihanna featuring Calvin Harris, Shum and Jenna Johnson set their quickstep to Mark Ronson’s “Valerie” featuring Amy Winehouse, a song performed by the New Directions during season 2 of Glee. Ahead of Tuesday’s semifinals, Shum confirmed he and Johnson were using the Glee arrangement for inspiration. “It’ll be sung by the band, the wonderful Dancing With the Stars band. And just that energy, feeling that for a quickstep … it’s gonna be beautiful. Can’t wait for y’all to see it,” he noted in an Instagram Story.

In rehearsals, Shum spoke about how “meaningful” the song was to Glee fans. “Glee definitely changed my life,” he added. “It gave me the opportunity to not only dance, but act. And I never thought I would be able to dance to that song again.”

Both of Shum and Johnson’s dances on Tuesday night earned perfect scores from the judges.

Shum began his career as a backup dancer for pop icons including Jennifer Lopez and Mariah Carey before starring on Glee from 2009 to 2015. The cast weathered a handful of tragedies through the years, including the deaths of Cory Monteith and Mark Salling in 2013 and 2018, respectively. We will make sure to keep your legacy and spirit alive so Josey will grow up to know the incredible woman you were. Love you, Naya. You are already missed. Eternally.”

#3559. How GTA 6 Is Eligible For The Game Awards This Year

We've known for some time that Grand Theft Auto 6 was likely to be eligible for The Game Awards, and now that 2026's TGA nominees are live, it's official: Not only is GTA eligible, but it actually has the most nominations of any game.

That's somewhat of an unusual situation, given that GTA 6 reviews are not yet live. Regardless, this invites some questions of how or why GTA 6 can be eligible before reviews go out and before the game is available. (Nominations even confirmed a key actor in the game.)

For months, the official website for The Game Awards has listed November 20, 2026 at 9 PM PT as the cutoff date for this year's ceremony, which means that any game that launches before that time can be considered for nomination. As GTA VI is scheduled to launch one day earlier, on November 19, GTA 6 is eligible just like any other game already released this year.

Now, before torches are lit and pitchforks are sharpened, evidence suggests that date was not put in place specifically for GTA to be eligible this year: The Friday before Thanksgiving has routinely been the cutoff for TGA nominations.

Last year, the cutoff was November 21, as referenced in this Polygon article regarding Dispatch's eligibility. In 2024, eligibility was cut off on November 22, as evidenced in this Polygon article exploring the games that missed 2024 and were eligible in 2025.

2018 was the last time a Rockstar project was eligible for most categories at The Game Awards, as Red Dead Redemption II landed 10 nominations and four wins. Notably, one of those wins was not Game of the year, which went to Sony Santa Monica for the God of War reboot.

Grand Theft Auto VI's eligibility for TGA 2026 was never in doubt--well, unless it got delayed again. Now that we're clear of that scenario, it's only a matter of time until we see just how many trophies are headed to Vice City.

Maura Higgins became a quick fan favorite on Dancing with the Stars, but I'm worried she could miss the Season 35 finals. With the semifinals and one vote before the finale, I'm afraid her run on the 2026 TV schedule may be at an end. Now, it seems I may have more reason to be concerned about what lies ahead.

I Thought I Knew Who I Wanted To Win DWTS Season 35. But One Comment Totally Changed My Opinion

#3557. This Fighting Game Is Nominated For A TGA Despite Development Shutting Down

Earlier today, Geoff Keighley announced all of the nominees for The Game Awards 2026, the annual celebration of gaming held in Los Angeles. Among expected nominees Grand Theft Auto VI, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and Control Resonant was one surprising name: 2XKO has been nominated for Best Fighting Game, despite Riot Games announcing the end of the game's lifecycle earlier this year.

Riot announced that "active development" for the fighting game, featuring characters from League of Legends, would end in December 2026. "Over the last few months, we’ve been monitoring 2XKO’s trajectory closely, and what we’ve seen is painting a clear, consistent picture," Riot said at the time. "While a lot of you jumped in to try the game and there’s an incredible community that plays every day, we haven’t seen enough players stick with the game to get to a path toward sustainability,”

Riot's fighter is joined in the Best Fighting Game category by Invincible Vs., Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, Avatar Legends, and My Hero Academia: All's Justice. 2XKO is also not the only game on this list whose future is in jeopardy; soon after it launched in April, Invincible Vs. developer Quarter up laid off reportedly 75% of its staff, while saying that future updates were dependent on the game's overall sales.

Grand Theft Auto VI received the most nominations for a single game at this year's ceremony with eight, including Game of the Year. Control Resonant and Resident Evil Requiem tied for the second-most nominations with six each, while Phantom Blade Zero rounded out the top three with five nominations. Nintendo earned the most nominations for a single publisher, meanwhile, with 12 across the event's 30 awards.

The Game Awards is set to take place December 10 live from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, California.

#3556. Musician Ryan Adams, 52, Is Engaged to Kate Farr, 22, After 6 Months of Dating

Country music star Ryan Adams is reportedly engaged to fellow musician Kate Farr.

“I’ve never been happier in my life. Kate is the most fascinating, kindest nerd I’ve ever met. She’s my best friend, and I’ve never been happier. Here’s to love,” Adams told TMZ on Tuesday, November 17. The outlet noted that Adams, 52, and Farr, 22, got engaged after six months of dating.

Us has reached out to a representative for Adams for comment.

The outlet also reported that Adams, who is the ex-husband of Mandy Moore, and Farr, a writer and producer who now works in the music industry, met through mutual friends earlier this year. “While the two started out as friends, things quickly turned romantic,” the outlet stated.

A photo of two hands was also published by the outlet, seemingly of Farr’s atop Adams,’ with the top donning a diamond set against gold on its ring finger.

Less than one month again, Adams shared his adoration for Farr in the comments section of an Instagram post she shared. The October 21 carousel, which included three close-up snaps of Farr demurely gazing off camera, attracted Adams’ comment, “Just stopping by to tell you I love you so very much and I hear you rattling around upstairs. ❤️.”

Farr wrote in response, “WEIRDO!!! jk I love you 💛,” which drew a string of red heart emojis from Adams.

TMZ also reported that Farr “moved to Los Angeles to be with Ryan … and the two are now living together,” with plans to leave California one day to move “back to the Midwest … to be closer to family.”

Adams was married to Moore, 42, from March 2009. In January 2015, the former couple separated and their divorce was finalized in June the following year. In the aftermath of her marriage breakdown, Moore alleged in an interview with The New York Times that she was the victim of psychological abuse at the hands of Adams.

The article, which included seven women’s allegations of emotional abuse and sexual misconduct against Adams, including Moore, stated that she was at a pivotal point in her own musical career.

“Music was a point of control for him,” she was quoted as saying in the February 2019 article. “He would always tell me, ‘You’re not a real musician, because you don’t play an instrument.’”

Moore, who is now married to fellow musician Taylor Goldsmith and shares three children with him, also noted that she would once write songs with Adams, which he promised to record but never did.

“His controlling behavior essentially did block my ability to make new connections in the industry during a very pivotal and potentially lucrative time — my entire mid-to-late 20s,” Moore said at the time.

The outlet noted at the time that Adams, through his lawyer, referred to Moore’s depiction of their relationship to be “completely inconsistent with his view of the relationship,” adding that he supported her “well-deserved professional success.”

He issued a further statement to Us in the hours following the Times article going live.

“I am not a perfect man and I have made many mistakes. To anyone I have ever hurt, however unintentionally, I apologize deeply and unreservedly,” the statement to Us read at the time. “But the picture that this article paints is upsettingly inaccurate. Some of its details are misrepresented; some are exaggerated; some are outright false. I would never have inappropriate interactions with someone I thought was underage. Period. As someone who has always tried to spread joy through my music and my life, hearing that some people believe I caused them pain saddens me greatly. I am resolved to work to be the best man I can be. And I wish everyone compassion, understanding and healing.”

Back in August, the public was devastated to learn that actress Hayden Panettiere died at age 36. This was a huge shock, especially considering her brother died just a few years earlier. Fans are still mourning and re-watching her work on projects like Heroes, and plenty of people were surprised when Panettiere's mother Lesley Vogel didn't attend her celebration of life back in September. Now Vogel is speaking out and explaining her absence for the services.

Fans still have questions about Hayden Panettiere's death, and were curious about why her mother wasn't in attendance for the late actress' funeral services. Lesley Vogel recently appeared on Inside Edition, where she explained why she chose to opt out of her daughter's celebration of life. She was quoted saying:

I just didn’t want to rock the boat either; it was probably for the best.

During the interview, she shared that she and Hayden Panettiere drifted away from each other after the Scream actress' relationship with ex Brian Hickerson started picking up. They mother and daughter seemingly had a difficult relationship, some of which was mentioned in the actress' memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning. Still, it was surprising for some that Vogel didn't attend the funeral services.

While appearing in the same interview, Lesley Vogel claimed that she was indeed invited, but didn't think her presence would be helpful during this difficult time. She went on to say:

I knew that some of the people there wanted to believe I was the horrible mother because Hayden was angry and made statements.

Clearly this was a complicated situation, which might explain why Hayden Panettiere's mother ultimately decided not to attend her funeral. She knew there'd be discourse about her either way, but is seemingly at peace with her decision. Inside Edition contacted Brian Hickerson for a comment, but did not hear back from him.

Panettiere's death hit the public hard, largely because she grew up right in front of our eyes, including early roles in projects like Remember the Titans and A Bug's Life. Millennial fans in particular grew up alongside her, and there was a ton of love her work on Ice Princess, Heroes, Nashville, and the Scream movies (the latter of which are streaming with a Paramount+ subscription). Folks were thrilled when she reprised her role as Kirby Reed in Scream VI, with Panettiere thanking fans who "came to her rescue". Clearly she's someone who meant a great deal to her fans, many of whom are still processing her death. As for Lesley Vogel, she's given an explanation for missing her late daughter's funeral.

Hayden Panettiere's legacy lives on through her various acting credits. Heroes is streaming on Netflix, while Nashville is over on Pluto TV. Our thoughts continue to be with her loved ones as they mourn and grapple with the loss.

#3554. BioWare Is Dead, But Mass Effect’s Spiritual Successor Exodus Just Gave Us A Glimpse of A Spicy Romance

For the first time since its announcement during December 2023's The Game Awards, players are getting a look at the female player-character from its upcoming sci-fi RPG Exodus--which was full of Mass Effect DNA back when we previewed it in September.

The default female version of main character Jun Aslan was revealed today via a seven-minute featurette showing off both female-Jun's face and a bit more of the game itself. The trailer also provided a glimpse of a brief romance scene between female-Jun and Suliman, who is one of the game's romanceable NPCs.

When GameSpot previewed the game, only male-Jun was playable, and we didn't get a chance to romance Suliman, but we did manage to earn his approval, suggesting he may be into both masculine and feminine Jun. We also didn't see the character creator, but there certainly appears to be one, as we see Jun sporting a different look during the romantic encounter with Suliman, with voice actress Carina Corti (Mafia: The Old Country, Little Death) providing Jun's voice throughout both scenes.

Jun's male character model recently got a complete makeover after players complained his original look wasn't pleasing to the eye, but up until today, it wasn't clear who was voicing him. Today, Archetype shared that Stephen Oyoung (Marvel's Spider-Man, Marvel's Spider-Man 2) will be voicing the character.

The female-Jun reveal is followed by a featurette called Scrappy Salvager, featuring a behind-the-scenes look at Jun's origins and the way players' decision can impact Jun's trajectory early on in the game.

"We think of players as the co-authors of our story, and that applies to Jun as well," game director Chris King explains in the video. 

Art director Mark Anderson describes Jun as a "little fish in a really big pond," rather than starting off as a typical hero ready to save the world. Additionally, the featurette goes into more detail about Jun's "precognition" ability, which allows them to see glimpses of possible futures. If interpreted correctly, these premonitions may help players make choices that benefit them. But misunderstanding them may lead to consequences that expand far beyond Jun and their friends. Due to the way the game's time dilation mechanic works, player choices can have unexpected effects that impact civilizations for centuries.

After the death of BioWare, it seems the Mass Effect formula will live on in Exodus, with its vast worlds, strange alien races, NPC romances, and narrative choices. It shouldn't come as a surprise, of course--Exodus developer Archetype Entertainment was founded in 2019 by BioWare veterans James Ohlen, Drew Karpshyn, and Chad Robertson.

Exodus launches on April 7, 2027 and is available to wishlist now on the PlayStation Store, Xbox Store, Steam, and the Epic Games Store.
